analysis.one_liner: Bans stock trading by members of Congress, Supreme Court justices, and top officials, and forces public disclosure of their federal payments.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to three House committees on the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar members of Congress, the President and Vice President, Supreme Court justices, and Federal Reserve officials from holding or trading individual stocks, futures, commodities, and cryptocurrency, requiring them to divest within 120 days. It would also require officials and their families to report any federal loans, contracts, or grants they receive, fix late-filing penalties at $1,000 per violation, impose a fine of at least 10% of the value of any banned holding, and move all financial disclosures to searchable public online databases with downloadable data.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens, who would gain the ability to see in a searchable public database when their representatives trade stocks, whether they hold assets that overlap with their official duties, and whether they or their families receive money from the federal government. Taxpayers also gain from rules designed to keep officials from steering government money toward their own holdings.

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits covered officials — members of Congress, the President, the Vice President, the Chief Justice and Associate Justices, Federal Reserve governors and bank presidents, and their spouses and dependent children — from holding, buying, or selling individual securities, futures, commodities, or cryptocurrency, and from taking net short positions, with required divestiture within 120 days [S2].
It would require officials and their families to report, within 30 to 45 days, any application for or receipt of a federal loan, contract, or grant, with a $5,000 fine for failing to report [S2].

It would replace the current cap on late transaction-report fines with a flat $1,000 fine per unreported trade, and impose a fine of at least 10% of the value of any holding kept in violation of the trading ban [S2].

It would require electronic filing of financial disclosures by members of Congress, top executive branch officials, federal judges, and Federal Reserve bank officers, published on official websites in searchable, sortable, downloadable form with public API access [S2].

It would close a disclosure loophole by applying the STOCK Act's disclosure rules to presidents, vice presidents, and directors of the 12 regional Federal Reserve banks, who are not currently covered [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress, the President and Vice President, Supreme Court justices, and senior Federal Reserve officials, who would have to sell individual stock holdings within 120 days and shift to diversified funds, Treasuries, or blind trusts, and who would face $1,000 fines per late trade report and fines of at least 10% of the value of any banned holding. Their spouses and dependent children would be subject to the same rules.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress and senior federal officials

drawbacks.text: The trading ban is broad: it covers not just new trades but all existing holdings, requiring divestiture within 120 days even for assets acquired long before office, which critics argue could deter wealthy candidates from running and force fire-sale divestitures, although the bill exempts diversified registered investment funds and Treasury securities [S2].

The disclosure penalties remain modest by design: $1,000 per late trade report and $5,000 for an unreported federal payment are small sums relative to a member's salary and assets, so enforcement would still depend heavily on press scrutiny and ethics office action rather than the fines themselves [S2].

A 180-day post-service 'cooling-off' period bars former officials from trading, but critics note officials can still make legally blurry transitions to boards and lobbying-adjacent roles once it expires, since the bill only restricts for-profit board service while in office [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit of barring lawmakers from trading individual stocks while they write the laws that move markets is large and direct, and the searchable online database would make conflicts visible to voters instead of buried in paper filings. The main cost falls on the officials themselves, in the form of forced divestiture into diversified funds, which is a real but modest burden given the bill's exemptions for diversified index funds and Treasuries. The bill's enforcement teeth — flat $1,000 fines — are deliberately modest, meaning compliance would still rely partly on transparency rather than deterrence. On balance the design is sound, though its breadth could be trimmed without losing the core conflict-of-interest protection.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees the day it was introduced, none of them ever took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Katie Porter introduced the bill on December 15, 2023 [S1][S4].
The same day, it was referred to the House Oversight and Accountability, House Administration, and Judiciary Committees, splitting jurisdiction across three panels [S4].
The bill attracted only one cosponsor in the House [S3].
No committee reported the bill, no hearing or markup is recorded, and no floor vote ever occurred before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Members of Congress, Supreme Court justices, and senior federal and Federal Reserve officials, who kept the ability to trade individual stocks and left federal payment disclosures unreported; House committee leaders also avoided a politically charged floor vote. Ordinary citizens gained nothing, since the disclosure and trading-ban rules never took effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Incumbent officials, whose trading stays legal

for.name: Katie Porter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the STOCK Act 2.0 banning stock trading by senior officials and requiring public disclosure of their federal payments

against.name: Chairs of the House Oversight, House Administration, and Judiciary Committees
against.role: Committee chairs with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill after it was referred to their committees on the day of introduction

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, and with only the sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor, the bill never drew enough support in either party to test whether the fight would split by party.

industries.industry: Members of Congress and senior government officials
industries.note: The bill would force these officeholders to divest individual stocks, futures, commodities, and cryptocurrency, pay $1,000 per unreported trade, and disclose federal loans, contracts, and grants to themselves and their families. They bore the entire cost of the bill, and no committee or chamber ever advanced it.
